blocks.text: They also hold that אשת eseth is the mole in these words of David, Ps. LVIII, 9, כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, which many of the Hebrews render thus: Like the abortive and the mole, they have not seen the sun. Among them are R. Selomo, R. Obadias Gaon on the Psalms, Pomarius in his Lexicon, and Elias in the Methurgeman, having no doubt been so taught by their forebears. For in the very Mishnah of the Talmud, than which the Jews have nothing, after the Bible, either more sacred or more ancient, the mole is called אישות esuth, a word derived from אשת eseth. So in the tractate Kelim, ch. 11, fol. 34a: מצודת האשות טהורה The net for the mole is clean. And in Moëd Katon, cited above: צדין את האשות ואת העכברים משדה האילן ומשדה הלבן כדרכו במועד ובשביעית It is permitted to hunt the mole and mice, both in a planted field and in an arable field, during the minor festival and in the seventh year. [col. 1031] And there the Gemara: מאי אישות אמר רב יהודה בריה שאין לה עיניים What is esuth? Rabbi Judah said: It is an animal lacking eyes. And a little later: מאי קרא כמו שבלול תמס יהלך כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, Why is it so called? (because it is said in Ps. LVIII, 9) as a snail that melts away, as the abortive and the eseth (or mole) have not seen the sun. And in the same place, in the Gloss, אשות esuth is defined as בריה שאין לה עיניים וחופרת בקרקע, an animal deprived of sight, and digging in the earth. Accordingly the Chaldee translator paraphrases [παραφράζει, paraphrazei] the passage of the Psalm thus: היך נפול ואישותא די סמין ולא חמין שמשא Like an abortive fetus, and the esutha (mole), which are blind and do not see the sun. [II, 448] It is certain, however, that this version has nothing sound in it. For the Hebrew words נפל אשת, which they render the abortive and the mole, mean nothing other than ἔκτρωμα γυναικὸς [ektrōma gynaikos], the miscarriage of a woman, as among the ancients Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and Jerome explained them very well. נפל nephel, for an abortive, takes its name from falling, like the Arabic سقط [saqṭ] sikt, or sukt. Nor does it occur only here, but also in Iob. III, 16. and Eccles. VI, 3. And אשת eseth, for woman, occurs more often in the construct state, but also in the absolute. So Deut. XXI, 11. And if you see among the captives אשת יפת תאר an eseth (that is, a woman) beautiful in form. And 1 Sam. XXVIII, 7. Seek me אשת בעלת אוב an eseth (or woman), a Pythoness. And Ierem. XIII, 21. Pains will seize you כמו אשת לדה, as labour seizes an eseth (or woman). So here נפל אשת is the abortive fetus of an eseth (or woman). Thus in these words there is nothing difficult, nothing ambiguous, nothing that could be drawn in different directions. And the sense too is perfectly plain. Those who are soon to lose the light of life are compared with the abortive fetus of a woman, whose enjoyment of life was so brief, and in so dark a place, that it never saw the sun. So there was no need to imagine a mole here, especially since it is customary in Scripture to assert of abortive fetuses the very thing the Psalmist asserts here, namely that they have not seen the light. So Iob. III, 16. Like a hidden abortive, I would no longer be; like infants who have not seen the light, which is added by way of explanation [ἐπεξηγητικῶς, epexēgētikōs]. And Eccles. VI, 3. 4. 5. The abortive is happier than he, though it came in vain, and went into darkness, and its name was covered with darkness, and it neither saw the sun nor knew, etc. Accordingly there seems to be an antithesis [ἀντίθετον, antitheton] in the words of Paul, 1 Cor. XV, 8. Ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί· [Hōsperei tō ektrōmati ōphthē kamoi], as if he were saying: “Christ was seen even by me, though in matters pertaining to salvation I was once as blind as an abortive is to the light of the sun.” Yet granted, though not conceded, that אשת eseth in the passage of the Psalm means the mole, even so they would not have what they want. For the words נפל אשת would mean the abortive of a mole, not the abortive and the mole, as they render it, supplying the conjunction AND, which does not appear in the text. Yet lest they seem to do this without precedent, R. Selomo here cites a similar passage from Ierem. XI, 19., where he would have the Hebrew words ככבש אלוף rendered like a lamb and an ox, likewise adding the conjunction. But we have shown in its place ^{f)} that nothing is to be supplied there, and that in Hebrew כבש אלוף is a tame lamb, and that الوف [alūf] aluph is still taken in this sense among the Arabs today.
